overview: EC2 (Elastic Compute Cloud) is AWS's Infrastructure as a Service offering: you rent virtual machines in the cloud and choose their sizing and configuration at launch. The section lists the launch-time choices (OS, CPU, RAM, storage type, network card, security group, User Data) and explains the EC2 User Data bootstrap script. These fundamentals underpin most SAA-C03 scenarios on compute, scaling, security and cost, so the terms here (EBS, ELB, ASG, Instance Store, security group, bootstrapping) reappear throughout the exam.

coreConcepts.definition: AWS's Infrastructure as a Service offering: the capability to rent virtual machines (servers) in the cloud.
The cloud model where you rent raw infrastructure such as virtual machines, and manage the OS and software yourself; EC2 is the AWS example.
Network-attached virtual drives used to store data for EC2 instances.
The service used to distribute load (traffic) across multiple machines.
The capability that scales services automatically by adding or removing instances.
The launch-time choices: OS, CPU power and cores, RAM, storage space and type, network card (speed, public IP), firewall rules and bootstrap script.
At launch you pick the instance OS: Linux, Windows or Mac OS.
Storage reached over the network rather than physically attached: EBS and EFS for EC2.
Storage physically attached to the host hardware of the instance, as opposed to network-attached EBS/EFS.
The set of firewall rules that controls traffic to and from an EC2 instance; configured at launch.
A bootstrap script supplied at launch that runs commands automatically when the instance first starts.
Launching commands automatically when a machine starts, to configure it without manual login.

mustRemember: EC2 = Elastic Compute Cloud = Infrastructure as a Service.
EC2's core capabilities: renting virtual machines (EC2), storing data on virtual drives (EBS), distributing load across machines (ELB), and scaling with an auto-scaling group (ASG).
Launch-time sizing/configuration choices: OS (Linux, Windows, Mac OS), CPU power and cores, RAM, storage, network card, firewall rules (security group), User Data.
Two storage categories: network-attached (EBS and EFS) vs hardware (EC2 Instance Store).
The EC2 User Data script runs ONLY ONCE, at the instance's FIRST start.
The EC2 User Data script runs with the root user.
Typical User Data tasks: installing updates, installing software, downloading common files from the internet — anything scriptable.
Security group = the firewall rules of the instance, set as part of its configuration.

keyComparisons.items: Network-attached storage (EBS/EFS) vs hardware storage (EC2 Instance Store)
keyComparisons.difference: Network-attached storage is separate from the physical host and reached over the network, while Instance Store is hardware storage attached to the instance's own machine.

keyComparisons.items: EC2 vs EBS vs ELB vs ASG
keyComparisons.difference: EC2 rents the virtual machine, EBS stores its data on virtual drives, ELB distributes load across machines, and ASG scales the number of instances.

keyComparisons.items: EC2 User Data vs manual post-launch configuration
keyComparisons.difference: User Data automates boot tasks at first start only, whereas manual configuration can happen any time after launch.

keyComparisons.items: User Data run as root vs run as a normal user
keyComparisons.difference: The User Data script runs with the root user, so it has full privileges on the instance.

commonMisunderstandings: User Data runs on every start or reboot — it actually runs only once, at the instance's first start.
User Data is a general-purpose remote shell — it is a bootstrap script executed at launch, not an interactive session.
Storage for EC2 is always physical/hardware — it can be network-attached (EBS, EFS) or hardware (Instance Store).
A security group is a networking device added later — it is one of the configuration options set at launch as the instance's firewall rules.
EC2 only provides the VM — EC2 as an offering also covers the related capabilities of EBS storage, ELB load distribution and ASG scaling.
mentalModels: Think of EC2 as renting a computer in AWS's data center: you pick the OS, CPU, RAM, disk, network card and firewall, then it boots for you.
Think of User Data as a note taped to the machine that it reads the moment it is switched on for the very first time, then discards.
Think of the security group as the locked door list for the instance: it decides who may come in and go out.
Think of EBS/EFS as disks connected by cable (network) vs Instance Store as a disk screwed into the chassis.
edgeCases: User Data executes at first start only — restarting or rebooting the instance does not run it again.
Because User Data runs as root, it can perform privileged boot tasks (installing software and updates) without extra permissions.
User Data content is open-ended: the source says it can do 'anything you can think of' as long as it is scriptable at boot.
Mac OS is offered as an OS option alongside Linux and Windows.
Storage choice is not a single option: you decide between network-attached (EBS and EFS) and hardware (Instance Store).

whenToUse.situation: A new instance must have packages, updates or files ready without logging in manually
You need a persistent virtual drive for an instance's data
Traffic must be spread over several machines
The number of instances must grow or shrink with demand
You need to allow or block specific traffic to an instance

patternsToRecognize.signal: 'automate at first launch', 'install software/updates at boot', 'configure without SSH'
'disk physically attached to the host' vs 'drive reached over the network'
patternsToRecognize.indicates: Instance Store vs EBS/EFS storage type

examTraps.trap: Choosing an option that says User Data runs on every boot or can be re-run by rebooting.
examTraps.correction: The User Data script is only run once at the instance's first start.

examTraps.trap: Assuming the User Data script runs as a limited user.
examTraps.correction: It runs with the root user.

examTraps.trap: Treating EBS or EFS as hardware storage.
examTraps.correction: EBS and EFS are network-attached; EC2 Instance Store is the hardware storage option.

examTraps.trap: Thinking the security group is configured after launch as a separate service step.
examTraps.correction: Firewall rules (security group) are part of the EC2 sizing/configuration options chosen for the instance.

examTraps.trap: Remembering EC2 as only 'virtual machines' and forgetting the surrounding capabilities.
examTraps.correction: EC2 as an offering also includes EBS virtual drives, ELB load distribution and ASG scaling.

beyondSource: EC2 User Data is supplied as text (often a shell script) and, on Linux, is executed by the cloud-init mechanism at first boot; the source states the once-at-first-start and root rules, which are the examinable points.
